42.context: Damascus melts at a bad report and her walls are given to fire; then Kedar and Hazor, a nation at ease with no gates or bars, learns that having nothing to breach is no security. Hazor becomes a haunt for jackals forever.
42.question: A nation with no gates thought itself safe because it had nothing worth besieging. What false safety does your own 'nothing to lose' give you?

42.title: I Will Shatter Elam's Bow
42.context: Elam's oracle alone in the chapter is dated like a sermon, to the start of Zedekiah's reign. The archer nation's bow is shattered, its people scattered to every wind, God's throne set in Elam, and the last line restores Elam in the last days.
42.question: Ammon and Elam end restored; Edom does not. What does the unevenness of these endings teach you about presuming on either mercy or finality?

43.title: Babylon Is Captured
43.context: The banner headline is lifted for all nations: captured, Bel shamed, Marduk shattered. Woven into the capture notice is the return: Israel and Judah together, weeping, asking the way to Zion, joining the LORD in an everlasting covenant.
43.question: Babylon's fall and Israel's homecoming are one event from two ends. What ending in your life is also a beginning you have not started reading as one?

43.title: My People Are Lost Sheep
43.context: The shepherds led the flock astray and the devourers excused themselves: we are not guilty, they sinned. God's answer is an evacuation order for His people inside Babylon and the old arithmetic applied: as she has done, do the same to her.
43.question: Who excused themselves for harming you with 'you had it coming', and what does God's answer to that excuse promise?

43.title: A Search Will Be Made for Israel's Guilt
43.context: Two lions devoured Israel, Assyria first and Nebuchadnezzar last, and Babylon will be punished as Assyria was. Then the record-office miracle: guilt searched for and not found, because God forgives the remnant He preserves.
43.question: Jeremiah spent forty years itemizing that guilt. What would it be like to have your own itemized record searched for and not found?

43.title: The Hammer of the Whole Earth
43.context: The hammer lies broken, the snare caught the challenger unknowing, and fugitives announce in Zion the vengeance for God's temple. The arrogant one is addressed personally, and the ground of it all is a Redeemer who pleads His people's case.
43.question: A pleading Redeemer is the legal opposite of an accuser. Whose voice do you hear over your case most days?

43.title: A Sword Is Against the Chaldeans
43.context: The sword is read down Babylon's whole hierarchy, officials, prophets, warriors, treasuries, and a drought falls on her waters. The lion oracle from Edom returns word for word, aimed at the empire, and the earth quakes at the sound of her capture.
43.question: The same oracle fits Edom and Babylon in turn. What word of God spoken to someone else turned out to be addressed to you?

44.title: Not Abandoned by Their God
44.context: The second Babylon oracle opens with a destroyer's wind and a reassurance: Israel and Judah are not abandoned, though their land is full of guilt. Babylon the gold cup, which made the nations drunk, is about to be paid what she deserves.
44.question: Guilt admitted and abandonment denied stand in one sentence. Can you hold both about yourself at once?

44.title: We Tried to Heal Babylon
44.context: Babylon falls suddenly, and her physicians resign in their own words: we tried to heal her, she could not be healed; her judgment reaches the sky. Israel's opposite report is vindication, and the Medes are aroused, vengeance for His temple.
44.question: The balm that could not heal Judah's neighbors cannot heal Babylon either. What patient have you kept treating past the point God called finished?

44.title: The Portion of Jacob Is Not Like These
44.context: Over Babylon the Creator hymn from chapter 10 is sung again: earth made by power, goldsmiths shamed by breathless images, and the Portion of Jacob, Maker of all things, named the LORD of Hosts.
44.question: Why does the oracle stop mid-destruction to sing about creation, and what does that pause do to the size of Babylon?

44.title: You Are My War Club
44.context: God addresses His unnamed weapon in a shattering series, horse and rider, man and woman, shepherd and flock, farmer and oxen, and names the purpose: repayment for all the evil done in Zion. The destroying mountain will yield no cornerstone for reuse.
44.question: The war club is God's, and the complaint about Babylon is Jerusalem's; both are on the record. What instrument of God have you mistaken for the enemy itself?

44.title: One Courier Races to Meet Another
44.context: The northern kingdoms are summoned, Babylon's warriors sit down from fighting, and couriers race to outrun each other with the news of a city captured end to end. Zion's voice closes the half: devoured, crushed, set aside like an empty vessel.
44.question: Zion's complaint is entered into evidence before the sentence is carried out. What complaint of yours needs to be on the record, stated plainly to God, before anything else?

45.title: I Will Plead Your Case
45.context: God answers Zion as her advocate: I will plead your case and dry up her sea. Babylon becomes rubble and a jackals' haunt, and God hosts her princes' last feast Himself, drunkenness into a sleep they never wake from.
45.question: God's vengeance here is conducted as a court case pleaded, not a rage vented. What difference does that make to trusting Him with yours?

45.title: How Sheshach Has Been Captured
45.context: Babylon's cipher name is used at her capture; the sea covers her; Bel is made to spew out what he swallowed, temple vessels and all. Through the sentence runs the standing order: come out of her, My people.
45.question: Come out of her is spoken to God's people living comfortably inside the judged city. What is your 'her' to come out of?

45.title: Do Not Let Your Heart Grow Faint
45.context: The exiles are braced for years of rumors and prepared for heaven's shout at the end. Those who escaped the sword are told to depart, remember the LORD from far away, and let Jerusalem come to mind, while their shame is spoken aloud.
45.question: Remembering from far away is the exiles' assigned work. What are you far away from that you are being asked to remember, not return to yet?

45.title: I Will Make Her Princes Drunk
45.context: A cry is heard from Babylon and great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans; her warriors' bows are broken, for the LORD is a God of retribution who will repay in full. Her princes, wise men, and warriors are made drunk into the sleep they never wake from, and her thick walls are leveled, the nations' labor gone to fuel the flames.
45.question: Retribution in full is a measured phrase, not a wild one. What does exact repayment by God free you from attempting yourself?

45.title: Tie a Stone to It
45.context: The oracle leaves the page and becomes an errand: Seraiah son of Neriah, Baruch's brother, travels to Babylon with Zedekiah in his fourth year, carrying the single scroll of all these words. He reads it aloud there, prays God's promise back to Him, ties a stone to it, and sinks it in the Euphrates: in the same way Babylon will sink and never rise again. Here end the words of Jeremiah.
45.question: Jeremiah's scrolls were burned by a king and sunk by his own order, and both survived in the book. What have you committed to fire or water that God preserved anyway?

46.title: Until He Finally Banished Them
46.context: The appendix opens with Zedekiah's accession at twenty-one and the reason given for everything: the anger of the LORD, until He banished them from His presence. Siege dates, the breach, the night flight, and the capture at Jericho follow as record.
46.question: The appendix gives the fall as record, not sermon. What event in your life needs to be written as record before it can be understood as sermon?

46.title: Every Significant Building Burned
46.context: Nebuzaradan burns the house of the LORD, the palace, and every significant building, breaks the walls, and exiles the city, leaving the poorest to tend vineyards and fields, the same poor who gathered at Mizpah.
46.question: The poorest were left to tend the land the kings lost. What has been left in your care that the powerful forfeited?

46.title: Beyond Measure
46.context: The bronze is inventoried on its way to Babylon: pillars eighteen cubits tall, capitals with ninety-six pomegranates on the sides and a hundred in all. Solomon's craftsmanship is measured one last time on the scrap carts.
46.question: Why does the record measure the bronze so carefully at the moment of losing it? What of yours deserves that kind of careful count?

46.title: So Judah Was Taken Into Exile
46.context: Priests, doorkeepers, officials, the scribe of the army, and sixty men are executed at Riblah, the chief priest Seraiah among them, not Baruch's brother. Then the exile is counted: 3,023, then 832, then 745; 4,600 in all.
46.question: The book that began with a boy's call ends its record with arithmetic. What do the small, exact numbers of a loss say that a round grief cannot?

46.title: He Dined Regularly at the King's Table
46.context: Thirty-seven years into his exile, Jehoiachin is pardoned by Evil-merodach, spoken to kindly, seated above the other captive kings, and given a daily portion for the rest of his life. Both Kings and Jeremiah end their books at this table.
46.question: The largest book of the prophets ends on a daily portion, not a restoration. What daily portion is God using to keep a hope of yours alive?
